newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine inflation fall seen broken by Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Philippine inflation fall seen broken by Christmas.

text.p: The Philippines' September inflation forecasts show that a year-long downtrend is still being sustained, but an extravagant Filipino Christmas could reverse the pattern in the last quarter, analysts said.
A Reuter poll on Tuesday showed a majority of analysts expected year-on-year inflation for the month of September to fall below 5.5 percent, down from 7.9 percent in August.
Stock brokerages were among the more optimistic in their forecasts, while a mutual fund expected inflation in September would be between 6.4 and 6.5 percent.
Philippine inflation has been on a downtrend since a rice shortage sent it above 11 percent in September last year. The rate was 8.9 percent in July.
"We expect a very bountiful harvest of rice," said Noel Reyes, research head of Anscor Hagedorn Securities, in explanation of why his forecast was lowest among the predictions.
Giving a forecast range of 4.8 to 5.2 percent, Reyes said prices of rice, an important ingredient in the Filipino food basket, had stabilised since harvesting began last month.
Erwin Tan, research manager at brokers Abacus Securities, predicted a range of 5.0 to 5.5 percent, while Alvin Ang, economist at brokerage All Asia Capital pegged his forecast at 5.1 percent.
"Our view of falling inflation is because of the base-effect from last year," Ang said, adding that the prices base had got distorted last year by a series of typhoons and an acute rice shortage.
The shortage and spiralling prices of the staple had taken inflation to a high of 11.3 percent in September last year and had turned public opinion against the government.
But Joby de Belen, general manager of Meridian Securities Inc, which runs the Philequity Fund, said he expected September inflation at 6.4 to 6.5 percent.
"If I see anything lower than six (percent) I'll be happy," de Belen said, adding that he thought the recent oil price increases would affect inflation.
"Many people think the price increases in oil have been very minor and six percent (inflation) is a good target, but in reality it could be different," de Belen said.

On August 8, Philippine Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson had said he expected September inflation to fall below 6.5 percent. He issued the forecast to allay fears of a possible jump in inflation after oil firms raised prices.
But the inflation rate, which has fallen continuously since last September except in one month, was bound to start rising from next month, the analysts said.
Ang of All Asia Capital, who predicted 5.1 percent for September, said the figure could be six percent in October, 6.7 percent in November and 7.2 percent in December.
The analysts, unanimous in their opinions about inflation rising from this month, put the blame on over-indulgence at Christmas.
"Particularly with farm incomes improving, you will see a lot more consumption this year," Anscor Hagedorn's Reyes said.
Filipinos say they have the world's longest Christmas party beginning in October and ending a week after New Year.
The claim has been validated by a popular shopping mall in Makati, which last week began sales of Christmas trees and gold-painted plaster-of-paris reindeer.
